chunks: Components on a SoC. The question: What are some components on a SoC?
A system on chip ("What is a system on chip") is built from separate blocks, and each block has one job.

It is easiest to remember them in five groups: blocks that compute, blocks that remember, the wiring that links them, blocks that talk to the outside world, and housekeeping blocks for clock, power, security and debugging.
Think of a restaurant. The kitchen does the real work (compute). The pantry and fridge hold supplies (memory). Corridors and waiters carry things between rooms (the wiring).
The front door and the delivery entrance connect to the outside (inputs and outputs).
The manager, the electricity supply and the wall clock keep everything running (housekeeping). Every room has a numbered door, which is how software finds each block on a chip.
Compute blocks (top) are masters; memory and I/O (bottom) are slaves reached through the fabric.
Around this core sit blocks that touch everything: PLLs and clock gating, reset, the power-management unit, security and debug.
CPU core: the general-purpose part that runs program instructions.
Accelerator: a block built for one heavy job, such as graphics, camera images or neural networks, that does it with less energy than the CPU.
SRAM: fast memory built right into the chip. DMA: an engine that copies data between blocks without bothering the CPU.
Peripheral: a block that connects to the outside world, such as a UART (serial port) or USB. PLL: a circuit that turns a slow, steady clock into a much faster one.
Take a small sensor chip. It has one CPU core, memory (SRAM) for working data, a block that measures voltage, and a UART to send results out.
A DMA engine moves the readings into memory so the CPU can do other work. A PLL takes a 24 megahertz crystal and multiplies it by 100 to get 2. 4 gigahertz.
Dividing that by 2 gives a 1. 2 gigahertz clock for the CPU. Everything sits behind numbered addresses, so software controls each block by writing to its address.
That is the whole idea.
"I group them by function. Compute: CPU cores with caches, a GPU, and accelerators like NPU, DSP, ISP and video codec.
Memory: on-chip SRAM, boot ROM, a DRAM controller and PHY, flash in MCUs. A bus matrix or network-on-chip with DMA and an interrupt controller ties them together.
Peripherals: GPIO, UART, SPI, I2C, ADC, USB, PCIe, Ethernet, camera and display. Infrastructure: PLLs, resets, power management, security and debug. All in one address map."
